proposer_argument.content:
POSITION
The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

EVIDENCE REVIEW
Claim A: The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child. This is supported by historical records showing that the CRC was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on November 20, 1989, through UN General Assembly Resolution 44/25. The UN served as the international body that negotiated, drafted, and formally adopted this international treaty.

Claim B: Poland created the convention on the rights of the child, proposing its idea in 1978. This is partially supported - Poland was indeed an early advocate who proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was among the first countries to support such an initiative. However, Poland did not create or formally adopt the convention itself. Poland was one of the first nations to sign the CRC when it opened for signature in 1990, but the actual creation and adoption of the treaty was the responsibility of the United Nations.

REASONING
The core issue is determining which entity was responsible for the formal creation and adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. While Poland did propose the idea in 1978 and was an early supporter, the actual creation and adoption of an international treaty requires formal action by an international body. The United Nations General Assembly formally adopted the CRC in 1989, making it the legitimate creator of this international treaty. Poland's role was advocacy and early support, not formal creation.

SOURCE BASIS
Claim A: UN General Assembly adopted CRC on November 20, 1989 (Resolution 44/25). Claim B: Poland proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was among early supporters/ signatories.

CONCLUSION
The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Poland played an important advocacy role and was an early proponent, but the formal creation and adoption of this international treaty was the responsibility of the United Nations General Assembly in 1989.

critic_arguments.content:
ISSUE
The evidence review cites UN General Assembly Resolution 44/25 as the basis for claiming the UN created the CRC, but it doesn't explain what distinguishes "creation" from mere adoption. The term "created" is ambiguous and could mean different things (drafting vs. formal adoption), and this ambiguity isn't resolved.

WHY IT MATTERS
Without clarifying what "created" means in this context, the evidence review assumes that UN adoption equals creation without fully explaining or proving this connection. This could confuse readers about what actually constitutes "creation" of an international treaty.

IMPROVEMENT
The evidence should clarify the meaning of "created" in this context and explain how UN adoption through Resolution 44/25 constitutes the creation of the CRC rather than just its adoption or signing.

ISSUE
Claim B mentions that Poland proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was an early supporter and signatory, but the evidence review doesn't specify what evidence exists for Poland being an "early supporter" beyond being among the first signatories when the CRC opened for signature in 1990.

WHY IT MATTERS
Without citing specific documentation or evidence of Poland's early advocacy role beyond their 1978 proposal, the claim appears weak and could be challenged for lack of supporting proof that Poland played a substantive early supporter role beyond the initial proposal.

IMPROVEMENT
The evidence should include specific documentation showing Poland's active role as an early supporter of the CRC beyond just their 1978 proposal, such as UN records, diplomatic correspondence, or historical accounts that detail their advocacy efforts before the treaty was formally adopted.

proposer_argument.content:
POSITION
The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child.

EVIDENCE REVIEW
Claim A: The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child. This is supported by historical records showing that the CRC was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on November 20, 1989, through UN General Assembly Resolution 44/25. The UN served as the international body that negotiated, drafted, and formally adopted this international treaty.

Claim B: Poland created the convention on the rights of the child, proposing its idea in 1978. This is partially supported - Poland was indeed an early advocate who proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was among the first countries to support such an initiative. However, Poland did not create or formally adopt the convention itself. Poland was one of the first nations to sign the CRC when it opened for signature in 1990, but the actual creation and adoption of the treaty was the responsibility of the United Nations.

REASONING
The core issue is determining which entity was responsible for the formal creation and adoption of the Convention on the Rights of the Child. While Poland did propose the idea in 1978 and was an early supporter, the actual creation and adoption of an international treaty requires formal action by an international body. The United Nations General Assembly formally adopted the CRC in 1989, making it the legitimate creator of this international treaty. Poland's role was advocacy and early support, not formal creation.

SOURCE BASIS
Claim A: UN General Assembly adopted CRC on November 20, 1989 (Resolution 44/25). Claim B: Poland proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was among early supporters/ signatories.

CONCLUSION
The United Nations created the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Poland played an important advocacy role and was an early proponent, but the formal creation and adoption of this international treaty was the responsibility of the United Nations General Assembly in 1989.

critic_arguments.content:
ISSUE
The evidence review cites UN General Assembly Resolution 44/25 as the basis for claiming the UN created the CRC, but it doesn't explain what distinguishes "creation" from mere adoption. The term "created" is ambiguous and could mean different things (drafting vs. formal adoption), and this ambiguity isn't resolved.

WHY IT MATTERS
Without clarifying what "created" means in this context, the evidence review assumes that UN adoption equals creation without fully explaining or proving this connection. This could confuse readers about what actually constitutes "creation" of an international treaty.

IMPROVEMENT
The evidence should clarify the meaning of "created" in this context and explain how UN adoption through Resolution 44/25 constitutes the creation of the CRC rather than just its adoption or signing.

ISSUE
Claim B mentions that Poland proposed the idea of a children's rights convention in 1978 and was an early supporter and signatory, but the evidence review doesn't specify what evidence exists for Poland being an "early supporter" beyond being among the first signatories when the CRC opened for signature in 1990.

WHY IT MATTERS
Without citing specific documentation or evidence of Poland's early advocacy role beyond their 1978 proposal, the claim appears weak and could be challenged for lack of supporting proof that Poland played a substantive early supporter role beyond the initial proposal.

IMPROVEMENT
The evidence should include specific documentation showing Poland's active role as an early supporter of the CRC beyond just their 1978 proposal, such as UN records, diplomatic correspondence, or historical accounts that detail their advocacy efforts before the treaty was formally adopted.

judge_result.reason: The United Nations formally adopted the CRC through UN General Assembly Resolution 44/25 on November 20, 1989, which constitutes the actual creation of an international treaty. While Poland proposed the idea in 1978 and was an early signatory, creating an international treaty requires formal adoption by an international body, which was accomplished by the UN. Claim B's evidence is also weak, lacking specific documentation for Poland's broader advocacy role.
